recent_posts.author: ILE_LABS
recent_posts.content_html:
Hi everyone,

We’ve published the first draft of Sigsheet, an open file format for signing a CKB multisig transaction. Each signer uses the wallet they already have: ckb-cli, Neuron, or an app built on CCC. We’d like your feedback before we write the implementations.

The problem

A CKB multisig transaction is usually signed by several people, often with different tools. Today two things get in the way.

  • Partial signatures don’t travel between tools. ckb-cli, Neuron, CCC and ckb-sdk each hold a partly signed multisig transaction in a different way. The incompatibility between ckb-cli’s tx file and Neuron was reported in 2024 (ckb-cli#584, neuron#3048). In our tests with ckb-cli 2.0.0, Neuron 0.204.1 and CCC 1.23.1, none of the three read another’s partial signatures: they were dropped on import, lost silently, or the file couldn’t be read at all (the measurements). So in practice, one person collects everyone’s signatures and assembles the transaction. Fiber’s 0.7.0 mainnet script upgrade this month, for example, gathered four of its five signatures from pull request comments (fiber-scripts#34).
  • A signature doesn’t cover the input cells. The multisig lock signs the transaction hash and the witnesses, and the transaction hash covers each input’s out point, not the cell it points to. A signer who can’t see the input cells can’t check the amounts they are signing.

What Sigsheet is

One canonical JSON file per transaction. It carries:

  • the transaction, with a witness template for each lock group to be signed;
  • the previous transaction of every input, so a reader checks every input cell offline, by hash;
  • the block headers and inclusion proofs a Nervos DAO withdrawal needs;
  • the multisig configs;
  • every signature so far, keyed by lock group and signer.

How it’s used:

  • Signers pass the file along, or each one shares a copy and anyone merges them. Any order gives the same bytes.
  • Whoever holds a ready file finalizes it into a standard transaction.
  • It works with the multisig locks and addresses already on chain: the genesis, 2024 and v2 deployments. There’s no new on-chain script.

The goal

One file that every signer’s tool reads and writes: ckb-cli and Neuron directly, and apps built on CCC through a separate package. Signatures then move between tools with no bridge in the middle, and nobody has to collect and forward them.

What’s published

All of this is in github.com/ILE-Labs/Sigsheet, linked at commits 4588a55 on main and e4896d3 on research so every comment refers to a known version:

  • The specification, first draft. It covers:

    • the file and its canonical form;
    • 31 reader checks, all run offline;
    • the message rule of each lock;
    • merge, ready and finalize, including a rule for the signature sets the genesis multisig binary rejects;
    • what a signer is shown;
    • creating and sending;
    • security considerations.

    Every rule links to its evidence.

  • Test vectors: 24 cases, 18 attacks and 2 mainnet transactions, rebuilt byte for byte by one command.

  • An independent check:

    • every message is recomputed with CCC’s and ckb-cli’s own code;
    • every signature is recovered;
    • every final transaction runs through the deployed lock binaries under ckb-debugger.

    The checks run on Linux, macOS and Windows.

  • The design record and its benchmarks, on the repository’s research branch:

    • every decision, with its evidence;
    • the paths considered, and why each was dropped;
    • the experiments.

What we’ve learned since publishing

  • On ckb-devrel/ccc#646, CCC’s maintainer closed the request: CCC currently has no plans to include Sigsheet, and further progress is welcome here on Nervos Talk. So we’re building it as a separate package on @ckb-ccc/core as published, with no change to CCC. The thread also asked why a new format is needed at all; the first question below answers it.
  • We’ve also shared it with ckb-cli’s and Neuron’s maintainers (ckb-cli#694, neuron#3518).

Two questions we’ve already been asked

  • Why not keep the partial signatures in the transaction itself? We tested that as our path D, and two design-stage measurements on Fiber’s 0.7.0 upgrade (a 3-of-5 multisig whose members sent five signatures) moved us off it. A witness with M slots can’t keep the signatures beyond M, and merging the five copies inside the witness in all 120 orders gave 60 different results (X3a, section 1). Sigsheet keeps every signature by lock group and signer: its merge gave the same result in 2,000 of 2,000 trials (X3a, section 2), and finalizes to the standard transaction (why path D was dropped).
  • Why not a hosted multisig wallet? A hosted wallet removes the exchange when every member uses it. Sigsheet is for groups whose members sign with different tools, such as ckb-cli and Neuron, on any of the three multisig deployments. A service like that could also read and write the same file.

What’s next: the roadmap to v1.0

  • v0.1:
    • the specification after this feedback;
    • a TypeScript library on CCC, the reference implementation;
    • ckb-cli commands, in Rust;
    • Neuron support through Offline Sign;
    • a demo on testnet with all three tools.
  • v0.2:
    • a readable summary for signers;
    • a ckb-cli command that writes the file and that summary in one step;
    • an optional relay that carries one signature at a time, about 367 bytes at design stage, instead of the whole file;
    • Neuron’s own Sigsheet screens;
    • Omnilock’s multisig mode;
    • support in more tools.
  • v1.0: a stable specification with a conformance suite any implementation can run, proposed as a CKB RFC.

None of this depends on any project including the changes:

  • the TypeScript library will work with CCC as published;
  • the ckb-cli and Neuron changes will be available as builds from the repository.

At design stage, each wallet’s change was small:

  • 381 code lines in ckb-cli, 229 in CCC and 137 in Neuron;
  • each wallet’s own tests gave the same results before and after (X6);
  • on a local devnet, ckb-cli, CCC and Neuron signed one shared file in seven flows, all committed (X5).

The feedback we’re looking for

  • If you sign multisig transactions today, for a treasury, a team wallet or script deployments: which tools do your members sign with, and which transactions? We’ll make sure the first implementations cover them, and once they exist we’d like to run one of yours through Sigsheet with you, on testnet.
  • Wallet and SDK maintainers: what would your signing flow need from the format?
  • Security reviewers:
    • the reader checks (§5);
    • the signature rules (§7);
    • the attacks considered (§13).
  • CoBuild and CKB IDL: the boundary in Annexes A and B.

@quake, @phroi: Fiber’s 0.7.0 upgrade, which you both took part in, gathered its five signatures from the deploy file and four pull request comments. It’s the case we most want to get right. A whole Sigsheet file for that upgrade is about 733 KB at design stage, far more than a signature in a comment. So v0.2 adds a ckb-cli command that writes the file in one step, and a relay message of one signature, about 367 bytes. Your view on how signatures should travel in that flow would help most. @doitian: the request-signature step you planned for ckb-cli deploy (ckb-cli#603) is the job we want Sigsheet’s file to do, and your view on what it needs would help too. @RetricSu, @rink1969: you’ve signed multisig transactions with ckb-cli and Neuron and run into their limits (ckb-cli#658, neuron#3260), and we’d value your view of the draft.

Every change the feedback leads to will be listed in the repository with specification v0.1, and linked from this thread.

Thanks for reading. We’ll answer every comment here.

— ILE Labs

topics.title: Unlinked for CKB: Tor-Routed RPC and Browser Privacy Extension

recent_posts.topic_title: Unlinked for CKB: Tor-Routed RPC and Browser Privacy Extension
recent_posts.author: Owais
recent_posts.content_text:
Funding requested: $1,000
Project duration: 6 weeks
Category: Developer Tools / Privacy
Target ecosystem: Nervos CKB
License: Open source
Applicant: Owais (GitHub: owaisdotcom) · Full Stack Software Engineer
1. Project Overview
Unlinked for CKB is an open-source browser extension prototype designed to improve privacy when interacting with Nervos CKB decentralized applications.
It adapts the anon-rpc architecture and browser-based Tor client (tor-js, based on Arti compiled to WebAssembly) to the CKB ecosystem. The goal is to let users route supported CKB RPC requests through Tor directly from their browser, without requiring them to install or operate a separate native Tor daemon.
The extension will investigate running the privacy worker in a sandboxed browser environment and integrating it with CKB RPC endpoints to provide Tor-routed blockchain access.
The prototype will implement two complementary features:
Tor-Routed CKB RPC: A browser-compatible transport that routes supported CKB RPC requests through the Tor network, reducing the ability of RPC endpoints to associate requests with a user’s direct IP address.
Wallet Privacy Inspector: A browser-based inspection tool that detects CKB addresses and recognizable wallet-related information in outgoing requests and shows users which external domains receive that information.
The project will focus on building a functional prototype rather than a production-ready privacy service. It will adapt existing technologies, develop the CKB-specific integration, test both features in real browser environments, and publish the resulting software with documentation and demonstrations.
The goal is to give CKB developers and users an early, usable example of browser-level privacy tooling, while providing a foundation for further development in the Nervos ecosystem.
2. Problem Statement
When users interact with CKB dApps, information can be exposed through both network connections and application-generated browser requests.
Network-level exposure
When a browser communicates directly with a CKB RPC provider, that provider can observe the connecting IP address. Changing RPC providers does not necessarily prevent this exposure.
Tor offers a way to route network connections through multiple relays, making it harder for the destination endpoint to associate requests with the user’s direct IP address. However, browser networking restrictions make a browser-native implementation challenging.
Wallet information disclosure
A dApp may transmit CKB addresses or other recognizable wallet information to external services through browser requests. These services can include analytics providers, application APIs and other third-party endpoints.
Users generally have little visibility into which domains receive this information.
Unlinked aims to address these two problems through a browser extension that provides experimental private RPC access and local inspection of outgoing wallet-related information.
3. Why Nervos CKB?
CKB’s Cell model and Lock Script architecture provide recognizable structures that can be used when inspecting wallet-related information.
CKB addresses encode information about locking scripts and their arguments. This gives the privacy inspector a practical starting point for detecting CKB-related identifiers in outgoing requests.
The prototype will investigate how to recognize these structures without accessing private keys or uploading users’ browsing data.
CKB also has an ecosystem of wallets, dApps and RPC-based applications that provides a relevant environment for developing and testing browser privacy tooling.
The project complements existing CKB infrastructure. A Light Client can independently verify blockchain data, while Tor addresses network-level IP exposure. These are different capabilities, and the prototype focuses on exploring the latter alongside wallet information inspection.
4. Proposed Prototype
Unlinked for CKB will consist of a browser extension with two main experimental features.
4.1 Tor-Routed CKB RPC
The first feature will prototype browser-compatible access to CKB RPC endpoints through Tor.
The intended request path is:
Browser extension → Tor-compatible transport → Tor network → CKB RPC endpoint
The prototype will investigate existing browser-compatible Tor technologies, including Arti-based WebAssembly approaches where practical.
Initial development will focus on:
Establishing a browser-compatible Tor transport.
Connecting to a configurable CKB RPC endpoint.
Routing a defined set of CKB JSON-RPC requests through Tor.
Displaying connection and routing status in the extension.
Handling connection failures without silently falling back to a direct connection.
The objective is to demonstrate that a browser extension can make supported CKB RPC requests without exposing the user’s direct IP address to the destination endpoint.
The initial prototype will use existing Tor technologies rather than attempt to implement the Tor protocol from scratch.
If an external gateway or relay is required, its role and operational dependencies will be documented.
4.2 Wallet Privacy Inspector
The second feature will prototype local inspection of outgoing browser requests to identify CKB wallet-related information.
The initial version will inspect Fetch and XMLHttpRequest traffic.
It will attempt to detect:
CKB addresses.
Recognizable Lock Script arguments.
Other identifiable CKB wallet-related values.
External domains receiving detected information.
The extension will display findings in a per-site privacy report.
For example, when a dApp sends a user’s CKB address to an external analytics endpoint, the extension will identify the destination domain and show the detected information.
The inspector will operate locally in the browser. It will not upload inspected request contents to a central service.
The initial prototype will focus on Fetch and XMLHttpRequest. WebSocket and other traffic types may be explored later, but will not be required for the first version.
5. Prototype Architecture
Browser extension
The main interface will provide connection controls, privacy inspection and per-site reports.
Tor transport
A browser-compatible Tor transport will be integrated for supported CKB RPC requests. The implementation will evaluate available WebAssembly and browser networking approaches.
CKB RPC integration
The extension will connect to a configurable CKB RPC endpoint and support a defined subset of JSON-RPC methods.
Request inspection
The inspector will analyze observable Fetch and XMLHttpRequest requests for recognizable CKB wallet information and associate findings with destination domains.
Local privacy reporting
Inspection results will be presented locally, without sending browsing or wallet information to a central analytics service.
6. Development Deliverables
The project will produce:
Browser extension prototype: An installable, open-source extension containing the initial privacy features.
Tor-Routed RPC prototype: A working browser-based experiment for routing supported CKB RPC requests through Tor, subject to transport feasibility.
Wallet Privacy Inspector: A working prototype that detects CKB addresses and recognizable wallet information in outgoing requests.
Per-site privacy report: An interface displaying detected wallet information and destination domains.
CKB dApp test environment: A controlled test dApp demonstrating wallet information disclosure and inspection.
Existing dApp compatibility tests: Tests against at least two existing CKB applications, documenting supported behavior and observed results.
Source code and documentation: Public repository, setup instructions, technical notes and a demonstration video.
7. Six-Week Development Plan
Week 1 — Extension Foundation and Tor Setup
Set up the browser extension project.
Investigate browser-compatible Tor transport options.
Evaluate Arti-based WebAssembly approaches.
Configure a CKB RPC test environment.
Define the initial RPC methods to support.
Milestone: Extension foundation and initial Tor transport experiment.
Week 2 — Tor-Routed RPC Prototype
Implement the initial browser-compatible transport.
Attempt to connect to a CKB RPC endpoint through Tor.
Add connection status and error handling.
Test routing behavior and prevent silent direct-connection fallback.
Milestone: Initial Tor-routed CKB RPC prototype, or documented technical limitations and an alternative implementation approach.
Week 3 — Wallet Privacy Inspector
Implement Fetch and XMLHttpRequest inspection.
Add CKB address detection.
Investigate recognizable Lock Script argument detection.
Identify destination domains.
Build the initial privacy report interface.
Milestone: Functional wallet information inspection prototype.
Week 4 — CKB dApp Integration and Testing
Build a controlled CKB test dApp.
Test the inspector against controlled wallet-information disclosures.
Integrate at least two existing CKB dApps into the testing process.
Record observed requests and findings.
Improve detection and reporting.
Milestone: Working inspection demonstration and initial compatibility results.
Week 5 — Prototype Integration
Integrate the working components into the browser extension.
Test supported CKB RPC requests.
Verify Tor routing behavior where implemented.
Improve the extension interface.
Address compatibility and performance issues.
Milestone: Integrated Unlinked for CKB prototype.
Week 6 — Final Testing and Release
Complete functional tests.
Fix remaining issues.
Publish the source code.
Write setup and developer documentation.
Publish the CKB dApp testing results.
Record a demonstration video.
Milestone: Public prototype release.
8. Success Metrics and Verification
The project will be evaluated through working software and reproducible demonstrations.
Tor-Routed RPC
Demonstrate a supported CKB RPC request routed through Tor in a real browser, if technically feasible.
Verify that the destination endpoint observes the Tor exit IP rather than the user’s direct IP.
Display routing status in the extension.
Demonstrate that the extension does not silently fall back to a direct connection.
Wallet Privacy Inspector
Detect CKB addresses in controlled outgoing requests.
Identify destination domains.
Display detected information in a per-site report.
Demonstrate local inspection without uploading request contents.
CKB Application Testing
Test at least two existing CKB dApps.
Document observed wallet-information disclosures and negative findings.
Publish reproducible test cases.
Open-Source Release
Publish the extension source code.
Provide installation and setup instructions.
Publish a demonstration and technical documentation.
The project will clearly distinguish implemented functionality from experimental or unsupported features.
9. Risks and Mitigations
Browser-compatible Tor transport
Browser networking restrictions may make direct Tor integration difficult.
Mitigation: Use existing browser-compatible Tor technologies, limit the initial implementation to supported RPC requests and document transport limitations.
Incomplete request inspection
Some wallet information may be encoded or transmitted through unsupported traffic types.
Mitigation: Focus the initial prototype on observable Fetch and XMLHttpRequest requests and document unsupported mechanisms.
False positives and missed disclosures
Not every detected string necessarily represents a privacy leak, and transformed data may not be recognizable.
Mitigation: Validate detections against controlled test cases and distinguish confirmed findings from potential disclosures.
10. Funding Request
Total requested: $1,000
The funding will support six weeks of prototype development, integration and testing.
The budget covers:
Browser extension development.
Tor transport integration and experimentation.
CKB RPC integration.
Wallet Privacy Inspector development.
User interface and reporting.
CKB dApp testing.
Documentation, open-source publication and demonstration.
The resulting software and technical documentation will be publicly available to the Nervos ecosystem.
11. Expected Ecosystem Impact
Unlinked for CKB will introduce an experimental browser privacy tool for the Nervos ecosystem.
For users, it aims to provide greater visibility into wallet-related information transmitted by dApps and demonstrate an alternative way to access supported CKB RPC endpoints.
For developers, it will provide a practical example of browser-based wallet information inspection and a test environment for evaluating application privacy.
For the wider ecosystem, it will contribute:
An open-source browser extension prototype.
Experimental Tor integration for CKB RPC access.
A reusable wallet privacy inspection component.
Testing results from existing CKB applications.
Documentation that can support further development of CKB privacy tooling.
12. Final Outcome
The final outcome will be an open-source Unlinked for CKB browser extension prototype demonstrating two complementary privacy features: experimental Tor-routed access to supported CKB RPC endpoints and local inspection of wallet-related information transmitted by dApps.
The project prioritizes functional software, reproducible demonstrations and practical developer deliverables.
The six-week grant will fund the development and testing needed to turn these ideas into a working prototype and establish a foundation for future improvements to extension browser privacy in the Nervos ecosystem.

Too many projects funded by the CKB DAO get built, then quietly abandoned. There’s no shortage of examples, and I’ll leave the names out of it. Worse still, some teams keep coming back for more money, dressing up the same project as a new proposal each time.
It’s just as worrying that a handful of influential voices can tip a DAO vote with a public endorsement. When a few big names can steer funding decisions, how much say does the wider community really have?
This is exactly the direction some community members warned about. I’ve seen people on X joke that CKB is a cash cow waiting to be milked dry. At this rate, the joke is starting to sound like a warning. I hope the community takes it seriously while there’s still time to change course.

recent_posts.topic_title: QuotaCell: Let your team spend without handing over the treasury
recent_posts.author: Ticoworld
recent_posts.content_text:
QuotaCell update: Off localhost and running on public Pudge
In my November 6 update, QuotaCell could finally complete a spending and recovery cycle through a browser. But everything was still running on a local CKB chain with disposable signers.
I said real wallets and public Pudge testing were next.
Well, we’ve made that jump.
QuotaCell is now live as a public Pudge testnet beta.
Website: https://quotacell.netlify.app
App: QuotaCell — Shared spending, owner control
GitHub: GitHub - Ticoworld/QuotaCell: Experimental native CKB policy for shared delegated spending, with verifier and isolated-node evidence. · GitHub
01_hero_live_desktop1920×1200 303 KB
Getting here wasn’t as simple as moving the app online
A lot of the work over the past two weeks has been dealing with things that didn’t show up in the local tests.
First was getting transactions prepared for real wallets like UTXO Global to review and sign, without QuotaCell holding anyone’s private keys.
Then came transaction recovery. A transaction could reach Pudge while the RPC response was lost, leaving the app unsure whether it succeeded. We had to preserve the original signed transaction and reconcile its outcome rather than risk submitting a second payment.
Even after deploying the website, I ran into another issue. My wallet connected, but the My Pockets section kept loading and eventually failed. Refreshing didn’t help.
We traced that to the discovery process rejecting normal indexer advancement, alongside the reliability problems of depending on one public RPC. Discovery now handles canonical indexer progress and can retry read-only queries through another Pudge endpoint. The regression tests passed, and I’ve confirmed Pocket discovery working again on the live site.
Getting the contract to work locally was one milestone. Making the whole experience survive real network conditions has been a different challenge.
What actually works now
An owner can create a Pocket, fund it, and give two independently controlled delegates permission to spend within a shared allowance.
Each delegate uses their own wallet, with individual limits and an approved recipient. CKB enforces the rules, rather than relying on the website to behave correctly.
The owner can adjust allowances, revoke or restore spending access, close the Pocket, and recover supported funds.
There’s also a public web app now, with Pocket discovery, transaction history, and English and Simplified Chinese support. You can inspect public Pocket activity without connecting a wallet.
And importantly, we now have actual Pudge transactions behind those claims.
On November 15, a documented nine-transaction lifecycle covered creation, funding, a 61 CKB payment by each delegate, revoking both delegates, closure, and recovery of a separate 73 CKB deposit made after the Pocket was closed.
On November 20, I completed another lifecycle through the real-wallet web app, including delegate payments, permission changes, and closure.
That second closure returned 78 CKB of protected funds and released 466 CKB of policy capacity, leaving the 134 CKB terminal Cell on-chain.
These were two separate testnet runs.
02_live_closed_pocket2160×1440 183 KB
The November 15 transaction record and capacity accounting are available on GitHub.
Here’s also a confirmed close transaction from the newer run.
03_pudge_evidence2160×1107 155 KB
Following up on the feedback here
Some of the earlier comments helped shape what I worked on next.
@ArthurZhang, you raised concerns about extra deposits, multiple fund Cells, and recovery getting stuck when unsupported Cells were present.
We’ve changed fund discovery to distinguish supported ordinary fund Cells from unsupported matching Cells, with local tests covering those paths. I still need broader adversarial testing on public Pudge before considering that fully resolved. Delegate and recipient rotation is also still missing.
@Ayoub_Lesfer and @psawyerberlin, I’ve kept the keeper refill and CSR discussion in mind.
Automatic refills aren’t implemented. And looking at the current policy’s capacity and payment requirements, I’m not convinced this version makes economic sense for small, frequent keeper top-ups. That needs validation before building a refill mechanism around it.
@RetricSu, you also raised the importance of keeping this approachable for small organizations and people who aren’t developers.
The interface has moved a long way from the original developer harness. But making it look easier and proving that someone unfamiliar with QuotaCell can actually use it are two different things.
That’s something I want to test with people outside my own setup.
Why only two delegates?
One thing I should clarify about the current design is that two delegates are the scope I chose for this version, not the number I think every team should be limited to.
I wanted to get independent signing, the shared allowance, owner controls, and recovery working together before expanding the number of participants.
Right now, the two delegate identities and their approved recipients are fixed at Pocket creation. You can update allowances and revoke access, but you can’t add a third delegate or replace those identities afterward.
For a small spending arrangement, that might be enough. For a growing team where members and recipients change regularly, it clearly won’t be.
I’d rather learn which flexibility people actually need before expanding the contract.
Where things stand
This is still an experimental, unaudited Pudge testnet beta, not something to use with real funds.
The current policy occupies 600 CKB while active, retains 134 CKB after closure, and has a 61 CKB minimum ordinary payment. Those costs are significant for smaller budgets, and they’re part of what needs improving or reconsidering.
But we’re now at a point where people can actually open QuotaCell, connect a compatible Pudge wallet, and inspect real transactions instead of relying on my local test reports.
What I’d really like next is for someone else to try it.
If you’re working on CKB, running a small project, or have a spending workflow that might fit this, I’d appreciate you taking a look.
I’m particularly interested in what confuses you, where something fails or takes too long, and whether this type of control would be useful for your own project.
If anyone wants to go through a small testnet scenario together, I’m happy to do that too.
Thanks again to everyone who’s shared feedback and challenged the earlier versions. A lot of the improvements came from trying to answer those questions properly.
There’s still plenty to work on, but it’s good to finally have QuotaCell out there for others to try.

recent_posts.author: NOrththebear
recent_posts.content_text:
1. Project Overview
Project name: MoniMkt
One-line summary: A reusable CKB lending validation toolkit, field-tested with real users against the MoniMkt testnet product.
Positioning: The primary deliverable is a standalone, reusable validation toolkit for cell-based lending markets on CKB. MoniMkt is the first reference fixture and field test, not the product being funded. This directly follows the committee’s suggestion to focus on a testing suite or validation tool without broader market operations.
MoniMkt is the CKB equivalent of what Compound built for Ethereum: a pooled lending market where users supply, borrow, repay, and withdraw against collateral. The difference is that MoniMkt uses CKB cells directly. Market state, positions, vaults, and the oracle are cells, and the rules are enforced by CKB scripts.
The market and frontend already work on testnet. What is missing is a reusable way to validate lending behavior across CKB lending products, and real product evidence from users who are not the builder. This proposal delivers both, with the toolkit as the core and MoniMkt as the first field test.
2. Committee Alignment
This proposal is structured around the committee’s feedback:
The core deliverable is a standalone validation toolkit, not a market operations package.
MoniMkt is one reference fixture and field test, not the product being funded.
The work is testing and validation only.
There is no security hardening, no oracle operations, no mainnet work, no custody work, and no ongoing hosted beta.
The entire scope is one toolkit plus one bounded field test.
The product field test exists to prove the toolkit is useful in practice, not to turn Spark into an operations funder.
3. Team Profile
Applicant / core developer: North Bear, full-stack and Rust, protocol and smart-contract development.
GitHub: GitHub - NOrththebear/MoniMkt · GitHub
Email: capc55005@gmail.com
Discord: northbears

Our operational and user-growth plan focuses on removing Fiber onboarding friction and targeting communities that actively need P2P ramps:
1. Targeting Markets Where P2P Is a Necessity
Instead of competing with centralized exchanges where they are already convenient, our primary rollout targets regions where CEXs are restricted, banking rails are fragmented, or strict KYC blocks everyday users from buying CKB. In these markets, non-custodial P2P via mobile money, local bank transfers, and cash solves an immediate, real-world problem.
2. Removing Onboarding Friction (LSP + Mobile Wallets)
The biggest barrier to using Fiber today is channel setup and inbound liquidity. Through Milestone 3 (our open-source LSP) and our collaboration with Cellula (JIT inbound liquidity on mobile), a new user won’t need to understand channel management just to buy CKB—they can scan a QR code from their phone or desktop and receive CKB directly.
3. Plugging Into Existing Nervos & Nostr Channels
Existing Fiber users: Integrating smoothly with Fiber Studio (which already has an active user base) and Cellula gives existing Nervos users an immediate place to use their channels.
Nostr network effect: Because Twine’s order book runs on public Nostr relays rather than a closed database, liquidity and offers are naturally discoverable across the Nostr ecosystem, not just inside a single app.
4. Ongoing Hub Operations & Community Support
After mainnet launch, I will continue running the public hub, maintaining the solver, and handling dispute resolution (backed by the 48–68 hour hold-invoice safety windows), while actively onboarding initial liquidity makers through our existing Telegram groups and X accounts so buyers always have live offers to match with.
Twine is meant to be an active, everyday utility for Fiber—not a repo left sitting on GitHub. If you have suggestions on specific communities or liquidity incentives we should explore, I’d love to hear them!

Clarifying Key Details on Twine: Dispute Protection, LSP Liquidity & Hub Compliance
1. How Buyers Recover Value if CKB Delivery Fails After Fiat Payment
Because fiat moves peer-to-peer outside Twine (via bank transfer, mobile money, or cash), Twine cannot reverse a bank transaction directly—instead, the seller’s CKB is cryptographically locked up front before the buyer ever sends fiat:
Pre-Locked Hold Invoice: Before a trade begins, the seller locks the CKB in their own Fiber channel by paying a hold invoice created by Twine. The seller cannot pull those coins back while the trade window is active.
Dispute Resolution & Solver Payout: If the buyer sends the local currency (with proof of payment) and the seller disappears or refuses to confirm, the buyer opens a dispute within the trade clock (48 hours for standard trades, 68 hours for trampoline/mobile payouts).
Cryptographic Enforcement: The hub operator reviews the payment evidence and instructs the solver to release the hold by paying the CKB directly to the buyer’s Fiber invoice. Crucially, the solver is cryptographically constrained—it can only pay the buyer or let the lock expire back to the seller; the hub operator cannot sweep the locked CKB into their own wallet.
Inbound Liquidity & Offline Buyers (LSP): In Milestone 3, our open-source LSP opens inbound channels for buyers on the fly and can use a hold-invoice buffer (bounded safely inside Fiber’s 4-hour default per-hop tlc_expiry_delta / 64–132 hour multi-hop TLC window) to hold the payout until an offline buyer comes back online. Until inbound liquidity is confirmed, the daemon keeps payment instructions closed so a buyer isn’t prompted to send fiat without a valid receiving path.
2. Regulatory Obligations for Hubs That Charge Fees
Twine is designed specifically to minimize custodial and payment-processing risk, though operators must still comply with their local laws:
Non-Custodial Architecture: A Twine hub never holds fiat and never takes custody of user CKB. 1. How Buyers Recover Value if CKB Delivery Fails After Fiat Payment

Because fiat moves peer-to-peer outside Twine (via bank transfer, mobile money, or cash), Twine cannot reverse a bank transaction directly—instead, the seller’s CKB is cryptographically locked up front before the buyer ever sends fiat:

  • Pre-Locked Hold Invoice: Before a trade begins, the seller locks the CKB in their own Fiber channel by paying a hold invoice created by Twine. The seller cannot pull those coins back while the trade window is active.

  • Dispute Resolution & Solver Payout: If the buyer sends the local currency (with proof of payment) and the seller disappears or refuses to confirm, the buyer opens a dispute within the trade clock (48 hours for standard trades, 68 hours for trampoline/mobile payouts).

  • Cryptographic Enforcement: The hub operator reviews the payment evidence and instructs the solver to release the hold by paying the CKB directly to the buyer’s Fiber invoice. recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CKB Escrow Security Test Kit
recent_posts.author: devnash
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @xingtianchunyan,
How the kit achieves generality. Three layers; only the middle one is per project.
Generic mutation engine. Starts from any transaction the target script accepts and changes Cell Model fields every script sees: output capacity, lock args or type; extra inputs or outputs; cell deps and dep groups; header deps; since (absolute or relative, and its metric); hash_type; witness bytes; occupied capacity; fee. Nothing depends on the source language or on escrow logic.
Small target descriptor. A TOML/JSON file declaring where the semantics live: which lock args hold participants, refund recipient and deadline; the cell-data layout; legal transitions; and invariants such as authorization, conservation, one continuation output per group input, and monotonic state. Without one, the structural mutations still run and are reported as review, not findings.
Invariant oracle. Built-in CKB invariants (capacity conservation, occupied capacity floor, since maturity, dep-group resolution, Source::Output binding) plus the declared ones. A mutant becomes a finding only when the script accepts it and the oracle shows value or authority moving to a party that should not get it.
The harness runs the compiled script through the standard CKB testing workflow and reasons per lock group and per type group, so it needs no source and works on scripts we did not write.
How it covers more than escrow. The six escrow categories are instances of four generic families: unauthorized spend, replay or double-settle, state-transition violation, and accounting or isolation violation. Any stateful cell script with a continuation output maps onto them — vesting and treasury locks, milestone grants, payment-channel or Fiber funding locks, subscription cells, restricted-transfer xUDT. The revision will demonstrate this with two adapters (the escrow reference and one non-escrow lock) and one third-party port, rather than assert it.
Limits. A signature lock refuses every mutation unless a signing hook is supplied; scripts that verify proofs or read external state need a statement-rebuild hook; one transaction is one code path; off-chain terms and who submits a refund remain application responsibilities.

recent_posts.content_text:
A second question I expect, about safety: should a third-party tool be building exit transactions for other people’s assets at all?
For a product that is gone, there is nobody else left to do it. The original team has stopped, so the real choice is between a public, reviewable tool and each holder piecing together raw transactions alone. Lifeboat is built to keep that risk small:
It never holds keys or funds. The holder signs in their own wallet.
Every transaction is shown in full before signing, and each output is checked against the locks the connected wallet controls, so anything going to an address that is not theirs is flagged.
In this grant, signing happens on testnet only. Mainnet signing waits for review.
Exits that need the operator (Godwoken or Force Bridge leftovers, USDI redemption) are labelled as such. Lifeboat points to the official process and never offers to “recover” them.
The code is open (MIT), and the release will be a static build published with its IPFS CID, so anyone can check that what they run matches the repository.
If the committee would prefer a narrower first step, for example read-only scanning plus the exit sheet, with transaction building kept on testnet until a review, I’m happy to adjust the scope.

Port c-kzg-4844 to CKB-VM; see EIP-4844 for more details.
We also introduce a blob tree built on c-kzg-4844. We already have SMT, but SMT proofs are quite large, especially when proving multiple elements at once. So we propose a new solution: the blob tree. At its core, it is a two-level path tree built on c-kzg-4844 with Shplonk. It commits to as many as 16,777,216 (4096×4096) elements in a tree of just two levels. Whether you query one element or many, the proof reduces to a single KZG verification call.
